source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
source.authors: Hoagy Cunningham; Aidan Ewart; L. Smith; R. Huben; Lee Sharkey

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures interpretability with automated prediction of feature activations on text and compares the results for neurons or basis directions and learned features. This is a different method from the Qwen3 neuron-pole audit.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports activation-patching results for indirect-object identification and qualitative feature case studies; these do not measure the versions here. The autointerpretability figure values are not stated in the text, so only the qualitative results described by the authors are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study scores directions, including the default basis and MLP neurons, by simulating activations. It compares top-and-random with random-only scoring, which bears on V6. It gives no neuron score values or shares, so V7 cannot be read.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim SAEs resolve superposition scalably, and that SAE features localise IOI behaviour with fewer patches than PCA. MLP results are mixed, with many dead features outside early layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse autoencoders and automated interpretation scores on Pythia activations, rather than auditing Qwen3 neuron poles and assigning proportions to job categories.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured advantage declines in later residual-stream layers. Random-only scoring gives significantly smaller scores than top-and-random scoring. MLP results are mixed, with many dead features and a larger active fraction in early layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse-autoencoder features get higher simulation-based interpretability scores than the default basis, random directions, PCA, ICA and MLP neurons. The advantage shrinks in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary directions are more interpretable than individual neurons or basis directions under automated simulation scoring, mainly in early layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual-stream basis directions are no more interpretable than random directions. A residual basis dimension encodes different information at different activation ranges.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-stream basis dimensions are not interpretable units in small transformers.

record.problems: The text does not provide numerical autointerpretability values for the comparisons, and the automated protocol uses small scoring samples. The authors note limits in automated interpretation, including difficulty identifying patterns involving previous or next tokens and inability in the protocol to verify explanations using model-output changes. MLP dictionaries can contain many dead features.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each method and layer from Figures 2, 9, and 10: the text does not give individual values, and the qualitative results recorded here summarize the authors' stated comparisons. Activation-patching and feature-case-study results were left out because they do not measure these claim versions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job-share counts.
No neuron-share estimates across models, MoE or scale; only Pythia-70M/410M.
No vision neurons or recursive-generalization analysis.
Does not test whether better tools or architectures raise the share of interpretable neurons; the SAE replaces neurons.
No neuron-based attribution graphs; circuits use SAE features.
Fraction of neurons with good simulation scores, and the effect of stronger explainers, are not stated in text.

missing.what: Statement that residual-stream basis directions score no better than random directions

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source (Bills et al.; the essay) is this paper. All scores are figure-only, so V7 cannot be judged quantitatively. The reader's V7 limits_scope label rested on R2, which compares the study's own method with baselines; it is removed.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not audit neuron poles or report the share with one job, two related jobs, or an unknown job.
It does not test whether the proposed shares hold across model sizes, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or models up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive-generalization explanation is tested.
The paper does not test the proposed architecture, regularization, and tooling explanation or the InceptionV1 interpretability estimates.
The paper uses learned dictionary features for circuit analysis, but does not test whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons suffice without a replacement model.
The tests use the paper's automated interpretation-and-scoring protocol, not an independent human assessment of explanations.
The paper reports autointerpretability scores but does not state the fraction of neuron explanations that meet a defined good-score threshold.

conditions.value: later layers; layer 4 and final layer specifically discussed

rows.baseline: ICA in layer 4; other comparison methods in the final layer

rows.subject: Pythia (model not specified for this result)
rows.operation_detail: The authors recalculate autointerpretability using randomly selected text fragments rather than top-activating fragments.
rows.measure: Autointerpretability score on simulated versus actual activations
rows.value: Random-only scores are significantly smaller than top-and-random scores; learned features still consistently outperform baselines, especially in early layers. Exact values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Significance is described qualitatively; numerical uncertainty not stated
rows.note: The authors explain that limited random samples can underestimate performance for heavy-tailed features. The scoring comparison bears on whether interpretations drawn from highly activating examples predict activations elsewhere.
rows.check: Subject should be Pythia-70M residual stream, all directions including the default basis. The drop is stated qualitatively, figure only. Authors say small random samples underestimate heavy-tailed features.
